evidence_items.locator: Opening paragraph; Methodology and Core Result sections provide sample and expectation details
evidence_items.explanation: Sixteen experienced open-source developers expected AI to shorten their work by 24%, but the experiment found longer completion times. This is a matched shortfall in one real workplace setting, not evidence establishing the breadth of Marcus's claim.

METR judged that developers likely benefited more by early 2026, while emphasizing selection problems and weak evidence about the size of the improvement. This limits extrapolation from e1 but does not establish whether earlier expectations were met.

evidence_items.locator: Paragraph beginning 'More than 90 percent of executives'
evidence_items.explanation: This research-publisher summary describes surveys conducted from November 2025 through January 2026: 89% reported no labor-productivity impact over the preceding three years. Its larger expected gains concern the following three years, so that comparison cannot establish missed expectations for the past.

evidence_items.locator: Section 'AI’s effects on GDP will take time to emerge', second paragraph
evidence_items.explanation: This prominent forecaster expected the measurable US macroeconomic effect to begin in 2027 and described productivity gains as dependent on widespread adoption over ten years. Modest gains before June 2026 therefore do not demonstrate disappointment against this forecast.

unresolved_gaps: No sufficiently broad comparison was found that matches earlier productivity expectations with realized gains due by the observation period.
The claim does not identify whose expectations define 'many people'; the matched developer experiment covers only 16 participants.
The broad firm survey compares past effects with future expectations, not past expectations with subsequent outcomes.
The official productivity release could not be read, and aggregate productivity growth alone would not identify AI's contribution.
